sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: Inspection (construction QA and QC) is the primary means of assuring micropiles are built to the plans and specifications; the chapter covers systems built under performance specifications. Construction monitoring may be by the owner, the contractor or both, depending on the contracting approach (Chapter 9); performance monitoring is usually by the owner. Short-term monitoring is usually load test measurements; long-term monitoring may be done for slope stabilization micropiles, where experience is limited.
sections.body: (p. 8-1) The chapter gives guidance on construction monitoring and inspection, i.e., construction quality assurance (QA) and quality control (QC) inspection, for micropiles. Inspection is the primary mechanism to assure micropiles are constructed in accordance with the project plans and specifications; short-term and long-term monitoring may be conducted to assess performance. Construction monitoring can be carried out by the owner agency, the contractor or both, depending on the contracting approach (method, performance or design-build, Chapter 9), while performance monitoring is usually conducted by the owner agency. The chapter describes inspection and monitoring of micropile systems constructed under performance specifications. Properly conducted QA plays a vital role in producing high-quality micropiles, since conformance to plans and specifications should give micropiles that perform adequately for the intended service life; it may evaluate (1) conformance of system components to material specifications, (2) conformance of construction methods to execution specifications and (3) conformance to short-term performance specifications. Short-term (during construction) monitoring is usually limited to measurements during load testing (verification, proof and creep tests), and may include ground surface settlements or movements of nearby foundations, particularly for underpinning. Long-term monitoring may be performed for micropiles used for slope stabilization, since experience with this application is limited, and may continue the short-term measurements.
key_points: Inspection (construction QA and QC) is the primary means of assuring micropiles match the plans and specifications
Construction monitoring by owner, contractor or both, depending on the contracting approach (Chapter 9); performance monitoring usually by the owner
The chapter covers systems built under performance specifications
QA evaluates conformance to material specifications, execution specifications and short-term performance specifications

sections.title: Inspection Roles Under Certain Contract Approaches
sections.summary: Method approach: the owner carries out QA against its comprehensive plans and specifications, inspecting for strict compliance; the contractor follows them. Performance approach: the contractor carries out QC, selects equipment and procedures and meets performance criteria; the owner does limited QA on materials, equipment, tolerances and sequencing. Design-build: the contractor carries out or is responsible for all inspection under an owner-approved QA plan, with random owner or third-party QA tests.
sections.body: (pp. 8-1 to 8-2) For micropiles contracted using the method approach, QA activities are carried out by the owner agency based on comprehensive material and procedural requirements of owner-provided plans and specifications; the contractor's responsibility is to follow the plans and specifications and provide quality assurance (as printed), and the owner's inspection assures strict compliance with each component of the specification. For the performance approach, the contractor carries out QC activities; the owner carries out a limited number of QA activities as required by the specifications, primarily to verify requirements for materials, equipment, construction tolerances and sequencing, and the contractor selects the equipment and procedures and is responsible for satisfying the specified performance criteria. For the design-build approach, all required inspection activities are carried out by the contractor or are its responsibility under the QA plan approved by the owner, with random QA tests by the owner agency or an independent third-party inspection firm.
key_points: Method approach: owner QA against its comprehensive plans and specifications; inspection for strict compliance
Performance approach: contractor QC; owner limited QA on materials, equipment, tolerances and sequencing
Performance approach: contractor selects equipment and procedures and meets the performance criteria
Design-build: contractor responsible for all inspection under an owner-approved QA plan
Design-build: random QA tests by the owner or an independent third-party inspection firm
sections.applicability: Who performs inspection under method, performance and design-build contracting.

sections.title: Pre-Project Preparation
sections.summary: The QA inspector must understand the project, specifications, inspection responsibilities (set at a preconstruction meeting), site and subsurface conditions and the function of the micropiles, and should discuss critical design aspects with the project engineer. The contractor's work plan must be approved before work: 19 elements from qualifications and ground conditions through equipment, installation plan, grout, reinforcement, postgrouting, utilities, load testing, calibrations, connections, remedial action and spoil handling. Figure 8-1 summarizes inspector duties.
sections.body: (pp. 8-2 to 8-4) Before construction, the QA inspector must understand the project and specification requirements, particularly inspection responsibilities, site and subsurface conditions, and material and construction requirements. Inspection responsibilities should be defined at a preconstruction meeting with the general contractor and all subcontractors (e.g., the micropile installation contractor). The inspector must understand the intended function of the micropiles and other system components, using the geotechnical reports, contract plans and specifications, and should contact the project engineer at the start to discuss critical design aspects and potentially difficult site and subsurface conditions. The micropile contractor's work plan must be submitted to the engineer for review and approval before any construction, and work shall not proceed until it is approved. It should describe at least: 1. contractor and employee qualifications; 2. the contractor's understanding of ground conditions and anticipated difficulties; 3. performance criteria and tolerances; 4. location and orientation of each micropile; 5. size and configuration (cross section) of each micropile; 6. capacity requirements for each micropile; 7. drilling equipment (manufacturer and model numbers), flushing media and precautions to minimize drilling deviations; 8. all equipment with equipment loads on the structure or adjacent ground; 9. general installation plan, sequence, phasing and schedule; 10. grout design mix and batching, mixing and injection techniques; 11. reinforcement sizing, configuration and corrosion protection; 12. postgrouting methods, procedure and equipment (if anticipated); 13. documentation and protection of existing utilities and other sensitive elements and measures to minimize impacts; 14. plan for low headroom or nearby obstructions; 15. load testing information (micropiles to be tested, type of test, maximum anticipated test load, allowable deformations, procedures with sketches of layout such as reaction piles and dial gauges); 16. calibration information for load cells, pressure gauges, dial gauges and other devices; 17. details of connection to existing structures; 18. remedial action plan for excessive movement of existing structures, spills to environmentally sensitive areas and other foreseeable hazards; 19. spoil handling procedures. Most importantly, protection of the existing environment, including underground utilities, must be considered; the contractor examines existing site conditions with the inspector and is responsible for equipment suited to the site. Figure 8-1 summarizes QA inspector responsibilities for a typical project.

sections.title: General
sections.summary: Specifications set minimum material requirements, explicitly or by reference to AASHTO and ASTM standards; prequalified products are not commonly required, though proprietary features may be involved (e.g., the micropile to footing connection). Conformance is assessed by (1) manufacturer or supplier certification, (2) product literature and visual inspection, or (3) conformance testing. All delivered materials are visually examined before installation; nonconforming materials are unacceptable unless corrected per the specifications or approved in writing.
sections.body: (p. 8-5) Specifications describe minimum requirements for micropile materials, explicitly or by reference to standard specifications such as AASHTO and ASTM. Because micropile materials are common civil engineering materials, prequalified products are not commonly required, although certain proprietary features may be involved in, for example, the micropile to footing connection. Recommendations for storage and handling of selected materials are commonly included in specifications. Conformance is commonly assessed by (1) reviewing manufacturer or supplier certification submitted by the contractor, (2) reviewing product literature and visual inspection, or (3) conformance testing. All materials and prefabricated elements delivered to the site must be visually examined before installation to verify geometry and dimensions and to identify defects in workmanship, contamination or handling damage. All nonconforming materials are unacceptable unless corrected in accordance with the specifications or by written approval of the project engineer.
key_points: Minimum material requirements set explicitly or by reference to AASHTO and ASTM standards
Prequalified products not commonly required; proprietary features may arise (e.g., micropile to footing connection)
Conformance by supplier certification, product literature and visual inspection, or conformance testing

sections.title: Storing and Handling of Cement
sections.summary: Cement comes in bags (43 kg/sack) or bulk bags (1320 kg). Store it off the ground and away from moisture (Figure 8-2), without stacking bags so high that the cement over-compacts. Examine it for lumps, hydration or contamination just before use. Mixing water must be potable and free of impurities harmful to steel or grout. Handle admixtures per the manufacturer and do not use them past their shelf life.
sections.body: (p. 8-5) Cement is typically supplied in bagged (43 kg/sack) or bulk (1320 kg/bulk bag) form, depending on site conditions, job size, local availability and cost. It should not be stored directly on the ground or anywhere it may absorb significant moisture (example of appropriate storage, Figure 8-2), and bags should not be stacked too high, to prevent over-compaction of the cement. Cement should be visually examined for lumps or other indications of hydration or contamination immediately before use. The water used for grout mixing must be potable and contain no impurities harmful to the steel or the grout. Admixtures should be handled with care following the manufacturer's recommendations, and approved admixtures past the manufacturer's recommended shelf life should not be used.
key_points: Cement in bags (43 kg/sack) or bulk bags (1320 kg)

sections.title: Storing and Handling of Reinforcing Steel
sections.summary: Store reinforcement above ground, protected from damage and weather, away from traffic; lift bars with fiber ropes or webbing supported at several points. Check size and corrosion on delivery; mill certificates are required, and mill secondary pipe needs tensile and chemical tests; Buy America contracts need US manufacture verified. Light surface rust is normal; deep flaky corrosion or pitting is cause for rejection. Encapsulated and epoxy-coated bars arrive pre-manufactured and need extra care (Figure 8-4).
sections.body: (pp. 8-6 to 8-7) Steel reinforcement should be stored above the ground surface and protected against mechanical damage and weather; bars should be lifted with fiber ropes or webbing and supported at several locations to prevent excessive bending. The contractor should take care in unloading and storing all reinforcing steel, in a protected location away from construction traffic. On delivery, reinforcing steel should be visually checked for size and signs of corrosion and should be accompanied by mill certificates; mill secondary pipe, for which mill certificates are not available, requires verification of steel quality by tensile and chemical testing of samples. For Buy America contracts, United States manufacture must be verified, and all steel must conform to the standards in the project specifications. Proper storage (Figure 8-3) prevents corrosion or contamination by dirt, oils and organics; wood spacers between the ground and the steel prevent slight rusting from contact with the ground. A light coating of surface rust is normal and indicates oil and grease are not present; deep flaky corrosion or deep pitting is cause for rejection. All steel should be inspected just before use. Double corrosion-protected and/or epoxy-coated bars should be delivered pre-manufactured (Figure 8-4) and handled and stored with extra care: epoxy-coated bars wrapped with padded bands on wooden or padded supports, pre-manufactured corrosion-protected bars stacked to avoid damaging the corrugated tube or epoxy, and epoxy repairs made per the manufacturer. Mechanical couplers, hex nuts, centralizers and spacers typically arrive in boxes, with mill certificates for the couplers and hex nuts, and are stored like other materials.

sections.title: Inspection of Construction Activities
sections.summary: Inspection of construction activities is treated under 8.5.1 Inspection of Drilling Activities, 8.5.2 Inspection of Reinforcement Installation Activities and 8.5.3 Inspection of Grouting Activities; no text is printed under this heading.
sections.body: (p. 8-8) No text is printed under this heading; see 8.5.1 Inspection of Drilling Activities, 8.5.2 Inspection of Reinforcement Installation Activities and 8.5.3 Inspection of Grouting Activities.
key_points: Construction inspection: drilling (8.5.1), reinforcement installation (8.5.2), grouting (8.5.3)
sections.applicability: Pointer to inspection of drilling, reinforcement installation and grouting (8.5.1 to 8.5.3).

sections.title: Inspection of Drilling Activities
sections.summary: Drilling must not cause unacceptable loss of ground (casing that cannot be withdrawn, much soil removed with little casing advance, subsidence above the drill location); the inspector records it. Remove temporary casing without disturbing the reinforcement, keeping it full of grout; keep drill fluid above groundwater. Drill, reinforce and grout continuously, in one day for bond zones in clays or weak rock that soften; plug open holes; keep casing 0.3 m above ground. Deviations beyond tolerance are design changes.
sections.body: (pp. 8-8 to 8-9) The contractor's drilling should not cause unacceptable loss of ground, indicated by inability to withdraw the drill casing, a large quantity of soil removed with little or no casing advancement, or subsidence of the ground above the drilling location; the QA inspector should document this and other observations in daily reports. Temporary casing removed during grouting should be withdrawn without disturbing or damaging the reinforcement or letting it lose contact with the in-situ soil, and the casing kept full of grout during removal to minimize drillhole collapse. The contractor is responsible for keeping the drillhole open; fluid levels in the hole must always be kept above the groundwater level to minimize ground losses from potentially unstable soils. Drilling, reinforcement installation and grouting of each micropile should be completed in a continuous series of processes as expeditiously as possible; materials such as consolidated clays and weak rock can soften when exposed to air or water, and there drilling of the bond zone, reinforcement installation and grouting of the bond zone should be completed in one day. Unless construction is continuous, the drillhole should be temporarily plugged or covered at the surface against debris and for safety, and casing (temporary or permanent) should be placed at least 0.3 m (1 ft) above the ground surface so drill spoils and flushing water from other operations do not contaminate the completed hole. Drilling spoils must be contained and disposed of per the approved work plan, and drill water controlled to prevent erosion and standing water. Micropile inclination and position may need to deviate from the contract documents, but a deviation outside the specified tolerances is a design change of which the contractor must notify the engineer beforehand; all deviations should be recorded by the inspector and reported to the engineer.
key_points: Signs of unacceptable ground loss: casing cannot be withdrawn, much soil removed with little casing advance, subsidence above the hole

Keep drill fluid levels above groundwater
Drill, place reinforcement and grout continuously; within one day where clays or weak rock soften on exposure

sections.title: Inspection of Reinforcement Installation Activities
sections.summary: Reinforcement goes in before grouting or into the grout-filled hole before temporary casing is withdrawn; the inspector records total pile length and bond zone length. It must reach its length without force: failure in an uncased hole usually means caving, requiring withdrawal and redrilling; driving or cutting off the bar is not allowed. Protect coatings and centralizers, check couplings and cleanliness, and confirm centralizers at the specified spacing, typically 2.5 to 3 m (Figure 8-5).
sections.body: (pp. 8-9 to 8-10) Reinforcement may be placed before the drillhole is grouted or into the grout-filled borehole before temporary casing (if used) is withdrawn; in either case the inspector records the total pile length and bond zone length of each micropile. The reinforcement must be insertable to its prescribed length without force; inability to reach it in uncased holes usually means soil has caved into the hole, and withdrawal of the reinforcement and redrilling is necessary. Driving the reinforcement to full length or cutting it off is not allowed. Corrosion protection and centralizers should not be damaged during installation, and no reinforcement (epoxy-coated, double corrosion-protected or uncoated) should be dragged across abrasive surfaces or through surface soil. All splices and couplings should be checked for proper seating, and the reinforcement must be clean of surface soil, oil, mud and other substances that may contaminate the grout or coat the bar. Centralizers and spacers should be checked for placement at the specified intervals, typically 2.5 to 3 m (8 to 10 ft) (Figure 8-5), and for attachment (typically tie-wire or duct tape) that keeps the bar centered. Tremie tubes placed after the reinforcement must not interfere with the centralizers.
key_points: Record total pile length and bond zone length for each micropile
Reinforcement must reach its length without force; in uncased holes failure usually means caving: withdraw and redrill
Driving the reinforcement to full length or cutting it off is not allowed
Do not drag bars over abrasive surfaces or soil; protect coatings and centralizers; check couplings are seated
Reinforcement must be clean of soil, oil and mud
Centralizers at the specified spacing, typically 2.5 to 3 m (8 to 10 ft), firmly attached (Figure 8-5); tremie tubes must not interfere
sections.applicability: What the inspector checks when reinforcement is placed in the drillhole.

sections.title: Inspection of Grouting Activities
sections.summary: Check grouting equipment and mix design first and the diameter of uncased holes; grout soon after drilling the bond zone. Tremie grout from the bottom of the hole until grout of injected consistency returns, in one continuous operation with a positive head in the tank. Pressure grouting during casing withdrawal stops if grout escapes at the surface; pressures are read near the injection point (Figure 8-6). Post grouting: monitor pressure and volume per sleeve; typical 2 to 4 MPa, documented above 6.5 MPa.
sections.body: (pp. 8-10 to 8-12) Before grouting, the contractor should check the grouting equipment and the grout mix design should be verified; the care taken in grouting greatly affects the quality and capacity of the micropile. The inspector should verify the diameters of micropiles drilled without casing. Ideally the micropile is grouted immediately after drilling the bond zone, otherwise before the hole degrades. Primary grouting injects cement grout at the lowest point of the borehole so the hole fills evenly without air voids: a tremie tube, typically tied to the reinforcement before insertion, pumps grout to the bottom until grout of suitable quality (the same consistency as injected) returns to the top; the tremie is then removed or left in the hole and filled with grout. Grouting should be one continuous operation with a positive head kept in the grout holding tank to avoid drawing air into the grout. Pressure grouting may be applied to the primary grout during casing withdrawal, with care to avoid distress to the ground or adjacent structures, and discontinued if grout escapes at the ground surface. Grout pressures are measured as close to the injection point as possible to account for line losses; typically a gauge on the drill rig is monitored by the operator during pressure grouting and casing withdrawal (Figure 8-6). With a hollow-stem auger, grout is pumped under continuous pressure with a grout head above the auger tip during withdrawal, and the auger withdrawn in a controlled manner to minimize necking. For post grouting, grout pressures and volumes must be monitored throughout the injection of each sleeve to prevent dangerous or needless over-injection and to verify the treatment progressively; post grouting pressures have been documented above 6.5 MPa (943 psi), with a typical range of 2 to 4 MPa (290 to 580 psi). Grouting records are described in Section 8.6.3.
key_points: Check grouting equipment and mix design; verify diameters of uncased holes
Grout right after drilling the bond zone, or before the hole degrades
Tremie from the bottom of the hole until grout of injected consistency returns at the top
One continuous operation with a positive head in the holding tank to avoid drawing in air
Pressure grouting during casing withdrawal: avoid distress to ground and structures; stop if grout escapes at the surface
Measure grout pressure near the injection point; drill rig gauge (Figure 8-6)
Hollow-stem auger: continuous pressure with a grout head above the auger tip; controlled withdrawal to avoid necking

sections.title: Required Project Documentation
sections.summary: Required project documentation is treated under 8.6.1 Micropile Load Testing, 8.6.2 Production Micropiles and 8.6.3 Grouting Records for Production Micropiles; no text is printed under this heading.
sections.body: (p. 8-12) No text is printed under this heading; see 8.6.1 Micropile Load Testing, 8.6.2 Production Micropiles and 8.6.3 Grouting Records for Production Micropiles.
key_points: Documentation: load tests (8.6.1), production micropile logs (8.6.2), grouting records and grout tests (8.6.3)

sections.title: Micropile Load Testing
sections.summary: The inspector verifies that the test pile was installed by the production method, the setup follows the approved working drawings and the test follows the specifications. During testing: never exceed the maximum allowable axial stresses, never drop below the alignment load, and plot measurements as the test proceeds. Check apparatus alignment, calibrated jacks and gauges, dial gauge alignment, travel and contact point, load magnitudes, sequence and durations, and interference points from pile deflection.
sections.body: (p. 8-12) During micropile load testing, the inspector must verify that (1) the test pile installation method is the same as for the production piles, (2) the load test setup follows the approved working drawings and (3) the pile is tested in accordance with the project specifications. General guidelines during testing: at no time should the micropile be loaded so that axial stresses exceed the maximum allowable stresses in the specifications; at no time should the applied load be reduced below the alignment load; and test measurements should be plotted as the test proceeds to identify unusual behavior. The QA inspector should check: testing apparatus alignment; use of properly calibrated jacks and gauges; dial gauge arm alignment and travel length; dial gauge point of contact; application of the proper loads and the sequencing and duration of each load; and potential interference points due to pile deflection.
key_points: Verify the test pile was installed by the production method, the setup follows the approved drawings and the test follows the specifications
Never load beyond the specified maximum allowable axial stresses
Never reduce the load below the alignment load
Plot measurements as the test proceeds to catch unusual behavior

sections.title: Production Micropiles
sections.summary: Comprehensive installation records establish the basis of payment and identify significant deviations from the Contract Documents. Table 8-1 is an example installation log for the contractor and inspector (design and as-built geometry, times, drilling log, grouting quantities and pressures); Table 8-2 is a completed example.
sections.body: (p. 8-13) Comprehensive records of micropile installation are required to establish the basis of payment and to identify potentially significant deviations from the Contract Documents. Table 8-1 shows an example micropile installation log for use by the micropile contractor and the inspector, and Table 8-2 is a completed example: a vertical pile with 177 mm by 13 mm casing, 57-mm by 15.5-m reinforcement, 8 m of casing below the bottom of footing with a 2-m plunged (cased) bond length and 6 m of bond below the casing, 16.5 m total length below the bottom of footing, drilled by cased rotary through gravel, sand and cobbles with full flush return; 12 bags tremie grout, 13 bags pressure grout and 2 bags after plunging (27 total) at w/c 0.45, with pressures of 0.55 MPa maximum (0.45 to 0.47 average) and 1.2 MPa after plunging the casing.
key_points: Installation records are the basis of payment and reveal deviations from the Contract Documents
Table 8-1 log: design and as-built inclination, casing, reinforcement, cased and uncased bond lengths, total length below bottom of footing
Table 8-1 log: drilling method, rig, bit, depth-by-depth soil or rock and flush return, and grouting quantities (tremie, pressure, after plunge), w/c, pressures

sections.title: Grouting Records for Production Micropiles
sections.summary: Record grout production and use daily, with the actual pressure and volume for each micropile. Strength: sets of three 50-mm cubes (AASHTO T106/ASTM C-109; Figure 8-7) at 3, 7 and 28 days, seven-day results the most crucial; 28-day requirements of 25 to 40 MPa are common. Take one set per 10 micropiles or per day per grout plant, whichever is more frequent. Density by Baroid mud balance (API RP 13B-1; Figure 8-8) at least once per micropile: specific gravity 1.8 to 1.9 is about w/c 0.45.
sections.body: (pp. 8-13 to 8-17) Because grout is such a vital component of the micropile, close attention should be paid to its quality and control: grout production and consumption records must be kept daily, and the actual pressure and volume of grout pumped for each micropile recorded by the contractor and the inspector. Unconfined compressive strength is determined per AASHTO T106/ASTM C-109, typically on sets of three 50-mm (2 in) grout cubes (Figure 8-7) tested at 3, 7 and 28 days; seven-day tests are the most crucial, since the grout typically attains the required design strength within that time. Cube strengths can be as high as 24 MPa (3,500 psi) after only 24 hours; a 28-day strength requirement between 25 and 40 MPa (printed as 3,600 and 5,800 ksi) is common for micropiles. The inspector verifies that cube strengths comply with the specifications. Samples should be taken directly from the grout plant; one set of three cubes is recommended for every 10 micropiles installed, or every day for each grout plant in operation, whichever is more frequent. Specific gravity of the grout is checked frequently to determine its water content, the prime control over grout properties: neat cement grout density can be determined per American Petroleum Institute (API) Recommended Practice (RP) 13B-1 by the Baroid Mud Balance Test (Figure 8-8), which is quick and inexpensive and should be performed at least once per micropile. A common specific gravity of 1.8 to 1.9 corresponds to a water/cement ratio of 0.45. Tests that assess quality before installation are more valuable since they permit immediate reaction to anomalies, whereas compressive strength values can be established 48 hours after sampling at the earliest. Pre-construction testing of the grout mix should be performed before production drilling, such as before and/or during verification load testing.
key_points: Keep daily grout production and consumption records, with actual pressure and volume for each micropile
Compressive strength per AASHTO T106/ASTM C-109 on sets of three 50-mm (2 in) cubes (Figure 8-7) at 3, 7 and 28 days
Seven-day results are the most crucial; cube strengths may reach 24 MPa (3,500 psi) in 24 hours
A 28-day requirement of 25 to 40 MPa is common for micropiles
Sample at the grout plant: one set of three cubes per 10 micropiles or per day per plant, whichever is more frequent
Baroid mud balance (API RP 13B-1; Figure 8-8) at least once per micropile; specific gravity 1.8 to 1.9 corresponds to w/c 0.45
Density checks allow immediate reaction; strength results come 48 hours after sampling at the earliest
Test the grout mix before production drilling, e.g., before or during verification load testing
